by: the lead's label for this run, 14 October 2026
run_caption: Miniature readiness evidence, not the demonstration. The analysis agent ran two rounds on the miniature development fleet, eight robot arms at two sites that we also used in development. The changes it adopted in round 1 stayed in force through round 2's regular work (the retained state). After the rounds the system froze the two procedures it wrote into a library (fingerprint 48619b468ceed7ad). This bundle makes no claim of transfer or reuse: no later fleet was investigated with these procedures.

opening.title: In short
opening.by: the lead, from the records of this run (14 October 2026)
paragraphs: An AI agent was asked to improve a simulated fleet of eight robot arms at two sites, working only from the fleet's records and from experiments it could request on the robots. It found that the second site's sudden drop came from a setting that delays the commands sent to its robots, and not from a camera adjustment logged on the same day for one robot there, and it tested both on the robots: undoing the delay setting clearly helped (on robot 8, 12 of 12 attempts succeeded against 4 of 12 without the change; on the site's other three robots, 10 of 10 against 3 of 10), while undoing the camera adjustment changed nothing (4 of 12 either way). It also suspected that robot 4's scene camera had shifted; recalibrating it gave 11 of 12 against 7 of 12, a difference too small to tell from chance on its own. It adopted two changes, undoing the delay setting at the second site and recalibrating robot 4's scene camera, and wrote two short procedures for later investigations, which the system checked and froze: one on telling a delay in a site's command path apart from a camera change made at the same time, and one on checking several repairs made at once on different robots without comparing a repaired robot against others that were also repaired.

The fleet was then measured on 64 reserved attempts that the agent never saw: the same 64 tasks, robots and starting positions, simulated once under each state of the fleet. These are 64 distinct cases measured in every state, not 256 independent ones. Before the agent's changes 31 of the 64 succeeded; after them 59 did. 28 attempts that had failed now succeeded ("rescued") and none that had succeeded now failed ("broken"), a gain of 43.75 percentage points. All of this gain came in the first round. In the second round the fleet did its regular work with both changes in place (102 of 104 attempts succeeded, against 149 of 208 before); the agent checked that its changes had worked, found nothing more worth changing and stopped, which is a valid outcome. A plan fixed after the first round alone therefore did exactly as well, 59 of 64, so this run shows no advantage of a second round.

This is miniature readiness evidence on a small development fleet that we also used while building the system; it shows the loop running end to end with a real model and real simulation. It is separate from the demonstration of adapting to a lasting condition and reusing the agent's procedures on another fleet, which is still running, and it claims no transfer to other fleets. The run simulated 440 new robot attempts (80 in experiments, 104 in the second round's regular work, 256 in the final measurement) plus 149 replays, a sample of attempts run again to check that the simulation reproduces them exactly; none failed, stopped part way or went unconfirmed. The agent worked in 4 sessions, with 41.4 minutes of model time and 190 tool calls (its requests to the tools that query the records and run experiments), and its usage was recorded completely. At the model provider's published API prices this usage would have cost between 38.60 and 77.20 US dollars; we ran it on a subscription, so that is an equivalent, not a bill.
